titel: Rye flour: why rye bread needs acid
kurz: Rye flour forms hardly any usable gluten network. Its dough holds together through gums that bind a lot of water, and it needs acid so [[krume|the crumb]] doesn't turn gummy.
bild_im_kopf: Like paste instead of a rubber band: it sticks and holds together, but it doesn't spring back.
was_passiert: Rye contains protein, but it doesn't form an elastic network like wheat. Instead it has a lot of gums (pentosans) that bind many times their weight in water and make the dough sticky. Rye [[mehl|flour]] also brings plenty of starch-splitting enzymes (amylases). They keep working in the oven until the starch sets, and can break it down to sugar. Acid from [[sauerteig|sourdough]] slows these enzymes.
warum_wichtig: Treat rye like wheat and you get a sticky dough and a loaf that stays damp and gummy inside. With sourdough, brief mixing and patience after baking it turns moist and sliceable.
faustregeln: For breads with a lot of rye: make most of the rye into sourdough, because the acid slows the enzymes.
Mix rye dough briefly rather than kneading for long: there is no gluten network to build.
Work with wet hands or a dough scraper, not with extra flour.
Let rye bread rest for at least a day after baking, because the crumb only firms up as it cools.
